heading.en: From ship to mouth to self-sufficiency

hook.en: In the early 1960s India depended on imported grain. Within about a decade it was producing enough food for itself. What changed on the farm?

title.en: HYV seeds and the two phases

body.en: The Green Revolution was the large increase in food grain production from the use of high yielding variety (HYV) seeds, especially for wheat and rice. *HYV seeds* needed fertilisers, pesticides and regular water. In the first phase, mid-1960s to mid-1970s, HYV use was restricted to more affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and mainly to wheat; in the second phase, mid-1970s to mid-1980s, it spread to more states and crops.
body.kn: ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಇಳುವರಿ ತಳಿ (ಎಚ್‌ವೈವಿ) ಬೀಜಗಳ ಬಳಕೆಯಿಂದ ಆಹಾರ ಧಾನ್ಯ ಉತ್ಪಾದನೆ ಭಾರೀ ಏರಿಕೆಯಾದುದೇ ಹಸಿರು ಕ್ರಾಂತಿ. ಮೊದಲ ಹಂತದಲ್ಲಿ ಪಂಜಾಬ್, ಆಂಧ್ರ ಪ್ರದೇಶ, ತಮಿಳುನಾಡು ಮತ್ತು ಮುಖ್ಯವಾಗಿ ಗೋಧಿ; ಎರಡನೇ ಹಂತದಲ್ಲಿ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ರಾಜ್ಯಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಬೆಳೆಗಳು.

title.en: On the board: How the Green Revolution worked

say.en: HYV seeds give big yields, but only with fertiliser, pesticide and regular water.
Phase one, mid-1960s to mid-1970s: mostly wheat, in Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
Phase two spread HYV to more states and crops.
Marketed surplus is what the farmer sells after keeping food and seed.
Fertiliser subsidies helped small farmers adopt, but critics say they now help rich farmers most.
On the board: How the Green Revolution worked.

caption.en: Move land from traditional wheat to HYV seeds. HYV seeds give big yields only with regular water and fertiliser. The family keeps what it eats; the rest is the marketed surplus. Yields are illustrative.
caption.kn: ಸಾಂಪ್ರದಾಯಿಕ ಗೋಧಿಯಿಂದ HYV ಬೀಜಗಳಿಗೆ ಭೂಮಿ ಬದಲಿಸಿ. ನಿಯಮಿತ ನೀರು ಮತ್ತು ರಸಗೊಬ್ಬರವಿದ್ದರೆ ಮಾತ್ರ HYV ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಇಳುವರಿ. ಕುಟುಂಬ ತಿನ್ನುವುದನ್ನು ಉಳಿಸಿ ಉಳಿದದ್ದು ಮಾರುಕಟ್ಟೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚುವರಿ.

body.en: Small farmers feared they could not afford the inputs and that HYV crops were prone to pests. The government gave loans at low interest and subsidised fertilisers, so small farmers also benefited. Subsidies encourage new technology, but economists argue that once a technology is accepted, subsidies mostly benefit the fertiliser industry and rich farmers and burden government finances.

problem.en: A farmer harvests 120 quintals of wheat. His family keeps 25 quintals for food and 5 quintals as seed. What is his marketed surplus?

answer.en: 90 quintals is sold in the market.

narration.en: Let us work through this together. A farmer harvests 120 quintals of wheat. His family keeps 25 quintals for food and 5 quintals as seed. What is his marketed surplus?

say.en: Let us work through this together. A farmer harvests 120 quintals of wheat. His family keeps 25 quintals for food and 5 quintals as seed. What is his marketed surplus?
Retained equals 25 plus 5 equals 30 quintals.
Marketed surplus equals 120 minus 30 equals 90 quintals.
So the answer is 90 quintals is sold in the market.

say.en:
Competitive exam practice: CUET-pattern questions. Read every option before you choose. Which of the following statements about the Green Revolution are correct?
A In the first phase HYV seeds were used mainly for wheat.
B The first phase was limited to more affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
C HYV seeds give high yields without fertilisers.
D Subsidised fertilisers and cheap loans helped small farmers adopt HYV seeds.
HYV seeds need fertilisers, pesticides and regular water, so C is wrong.
The other statements follow NCERT.
